title: How the immune system remembers germs
examples: How does the immune system remember germs?
Why do you only get chickenpox once?

explain.say: Your immune system can remember germs it has met before. That memory is why many illnesses, like chickenpox, usually only make you ill once.

explain.say: The first time a new germ gets in, only a few of your white blood cells happen to have the right shape of receptor to recognise it. Building up an army takes a week or two, so you may feel ill.

faq.a: Memory cells are long-lived white blood cells left behind after an infection. They remember the shape of a germ, so if it comes back they multiply and attack it quickly.
asks: How does the immune system remember?
How long do memory cells last?

faq.a: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by white blood cells called B cells. Each fits one germ's shape, sticks to it, and marks it so other immune cells can destroy it.

faq.q: Why does the first infection take longer to fight?
faq.a: At first, only a few white blood cells can recognise a new germ. They must be found, multiply and make antibodies, which takes about one to two weeks.
asks: Why do you feel ill the first time?
How long does the immune system take?

faq.q: How does the body find the right cell to fight a germ?
faq.a: Your body makes millions of B cells and T cells, each with a slightly different receptor. When a germ arrives, the few whose receptors fit it are switched on and copied many times.
asks: How do white blood cells recognise germs?

faq.q: Why do you only get chickenpox once?
faq.a: After chickenpox, memory cells for that virus stay in your body. If you meet it again, they act so fast that you usually do not get ill. Vaccines use the same memory, by showing the immune system a harmless version first.
asks: Why can't you catch some illnesses twice?
How do vaccines use immune memory?

facts: A first immune response to a new germ typically takes around one to two weeks to peak.
Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins made by B cells.
Some memory cells can last for decades, even a lifetime.
